Imputing new data

2026-11-16

Source: vignettes/newdata.Rmd
newdata.Rmd

Introduction

An imputation model is usually fitted and used on the same data. In prediction, the situation is different. We fit the imputation model once on training data, and later apply it to new cases, for example new patients for whom we want a prediction. The imputation model for the new cases should be the one fitted on the training data. It should not change because new cases come in.

mice.mids() does this with the argument newdata. It adds the new cases to a mids object, imputes their missing values with the trained imputation model, and returns the imputations for the new cases. The new cases do not influence the imputation model.

This vignette shows how to use newdata, which imputation methods mice.mids() uses for the new cases, and what to watch out for. See van Buuren (2018) for multiple imputation in general.

library(mice)

Basic use

We use the first 20 rows of nhanes as training data, and the last 5 rows as new data.

train <- nhanes[1:20, ]
newdata <- nhanes[21:25, ]
newdata
#>    age  bmi hyp chl
#> 21   1   NA  NA  NA
#> 22   1 33.2   1 229
#> 23   1 27.5   1 131
#> 24   3 24.9   1  NA
#> 25   2 27.4   1 186

First, we fit the imputation model on the training data:

imp <- mice(train, m = 5, seed = 1, print = FALSE)

Then we pass the new cases to mice.mids():

imp.new <- mice.mids(imp, newdata = newdata, maxit = 5, print = FALSE)
complete(imp.new, 1)
#>    age  bmi hyp chl
#> 21   1 30.1   1 184
#> 22   1 33.2   1 229
#> 23   1 27.5   1 131
#> 24   3 24.9   1 218
#> 25   2 27.4   1 186

The result is an ordinary mids object with only the new cases. Methods like complete() and with() work as usual. Internally, mice.mids() appends the new cases to the training data and runs maxit more iterations of the Gibbs sampler. The new cases are marked by the ignore argument of mice(). Their values are imputed, but not used to fit the imputation models.

The default of maxit in mice.mids() is 1, which is meant for adding an iteration to an existing solution. For new data, use a few more iterations, so that the imputations of the new cases can converge.

The methods come from the trained model

mice.mids() imputes the new cases with the imputation methods of the trained model, and does not choose them anew for newdata:

imp$method
#>   age   bmi   hyp   chl 
#>    "" "pmm" "pmm" "pmm"
imp.new$method
#>   age   bmi   hyp   chl 
#>    "" "pmm" "pmm" "pmm"

This holds since mice 3.19.8. Training and deployment then use the same imputation model. Earlier versions chose the methods again for newdata, which could give a different model.

Variables that were complete in the training data

mice() gives a variable without missing values the method "". In the training data, age is complete:

imp$method["age"]
#> age 
#>  ""

The new cases may still have a missing value in such a variable. Below, age is missing for one new case:

newdata2 <- newdata
newdata2[2, "age"] <- NA

mice.mids() then assigns the default method for the type of the variable, here pmm, and says so in a message:

imp.new2 <- mice.mids(imp, newdata = newdata2, maxit = 5, print = FALSE)
#> `newdata` has missing values in `age`, which had no missing values in the training data. Imputing by "pmm".
imp.new2$method
#>   age   bmi   hyp   chl 
#> "pmm" "pmm" "pmm" "pmm"
complete(imp.new2, 1)
#>    age  bmi hyp chl
#> 21   1 28.7   1 238
#> 22   1 33.2   1 229
#> 23   1 27.5   1 131
#> 24   3 24.9   1 184
#> 25   2 27.4   1 186

The predictors of age come from the predictorMatrix of the trained model. The model for age is fitted on the training data, where age is observed.

For a factor, the default method is logreg, polyreg or polr, depending on the number of levels and whether the factor is ordered, in the same way as in make.method().

Without this rule, the missing age would stay NA. Because age is a predictor of the other variables, the NA could then also stop the imputation of these variables for the same case. mice 3.19.8 to 3.19.16 left such values NA without a warning.

Leaving a variable unimputed

Sometimes we do not want to impute a variable in the new data. Set its method to "" in the trained model. Below, bmi is not imputed:

imp0 <- imp
imp0$method["bmi"] <- ""

A missing bmi then stays NA. Because bmi is a predictor of the other variables, also remove it as a predictor. Otherwise, the NA in bmi stops the imputation of the other variables for the same case:

imp0$predictorMatrix[, "bmi"] <- 0
imp.new0 <- mice.mids(imp0, newdata = newdata, maxit = 5, print = FALSE)
imp.new0$method
#>   age   bmi   hyp   chl 
#>    ""    "" "pmm" "pmm"
complete(imp.new0, 1)
#>    age  bmi hyp chl
#> 21   1   NA   1 199
#> 22   1 33.2   1 229
#> 23   1 27.5   1 131
#> 24   3 24.9   1 284
#> 25   2 27.4   1 186

mice.mids() keeps a method "" that you set for a variable with missing values in the training data, here bmi. It only assigns a method to a variable that was complete in the training data.

Models specified by formulas or blocks

With formulas or blocks, the imputation model need not include all variables. Below, age has no formula:

imp.f <- mice(
  train,
  formulas = list(
    bmi = bmi ~ age + chl,
    hyp = hyp ~ age,
    chl = chl ~ age + bmi
  ),
  m = 5, seed = 1, print = FALSE
)
imp.f$method
#>   bmi   hyp   chl 
#> "pmm" "pmm" "pmm"

A variable outside the blocks has no imputation model, so a missing value in the new data stays NA:

imp.newf <- mice.mids(imp.f, newdata = newdata2, maxit = 5, print = FALSE)
complete(imp.newf, 1)
#>    age  bmi hyp chl
#> 21   1 30.1   1 238
#> 22  NA 33.2   1 229
#> 23   1 27.5   1 131
#> 24   3 24.9   1 206
#> 25   2 27.4   1 186

Add a formula for such a variable to the training model if it should be imputed in new data.

Things to watch out for

  • The new data need the same variables. newdata must have the same columns as the training data, with the same types. Factors should also have the same levels. mice.mids() does not check this, and a different set of levels can give a confusing warning or wrong imputations.
  • Setting a factor value to NA. In R, newdata$age <- NA replaces the whole column by a logical NA, so a factor is no longer a factor. Use newdata[i, "age"] <- NA to keep the type.
  • Reproducibility. mice.mids() continues from the random number state stored in the trained model. Two calls with the same object and the same newdata give the same imputations.
  • The imputations of the training data are not returned. If you need them, use the mids object of the training data.

References

van Buuren, Stef. 2018. Flexible Imputation of Missing Data. 2nd ed. Interdisciplinary Statistics Series. Chapman and Hall/CRC. https://doi.org/10.1201/9780429492259.
